questions.prompt: A student who already finished an Azure-focused course in this catalog assumes they can learn AWS fastest by mapping every service directly onto its closest Azure equivalent. Per Lesson 1, why does this course push back on that approach?
options: AWS has its own service boundaries, naming conventions, and idioms taught on their own terms, even though some underlying ideas — like object storage or IAM's core concepts — genuinely do transfer directly
Because no Azure concept has any equivalent in AWS at all
Because the AWS console and the Azure portal use entirely different programming languages
Because this course assumes the student has no prior cloud experience of any kind, Azure or otherwise
questions.explain: Lesson 1 is explicit that some ideas really do transfer (object storage is object storage, IAM's core concepts are genuinely similar to Entra ID's), but AWS has its own service boundaries and idioms that deserve to be learned on their own terms rather than treated as a one-to-one translation exercise.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AWS Regions and Availability Zones, per Lesson 2.
options: A Region is a fully independent, isolated AWS deployment — an outage in one Region doesn't cascade into another
Each Availability Zone within a Region has its own independent power, cooling, and networking
The AZ letter shown in the console, like us-east-1a, refers to the exact same physical building for every AWS account
An Edge Location runs EC2 instances and most other AWS services, just like a small Region would
Choosing a Region for a workload usually comes down to latency, data residency/compliance, and service or pricing availability
questions.explain: Regions are fully independent and isolated, and each AZ inside one has its own power, cooling, and networking. The letter AWS shows you is randomized per account specifically so it does NOT line up across accounts — AWS exposes a separate, stable AZ ID for that. An Edge Location isn't a small Region at all; it doesn't run EC2 or most services, only caching/DNS for services like CloudFront and Route 53. Region choice does come down to latency, residency/compliance, and service/pricing availability, exactly as Lesson 2 states.

questions.prompt: A teammate created an EC2 instance in us-east-1 yesterday. Today, the EC2 dashboard in the console shows no instances at all. Per Lesson 3, what's the single most likely explanation?
options: The Region selector in the top-right corner of the console is currently set to a Region other than us-east-1
EC2 instances are automatically deleted after 24 hours
Since IAM is a global service, the EC2 dashboard should show every instance regardless of Region, so the instance must have been deleted
The Services search bar has to be used before any existing instance can be displayed
questions.explain: Almost everything in the console, including the EC2 dashboard, is scoped to whichever Region is currently selected. An instance created in us-east-1 simply won't appear if the selector is switched to a different Region — Lesson 3 calls this out as one of the most common sources of 'my resource disappeared' confusion for new AWS users.

questions.prompt: Match each AWS accounts and Organizations term to what it actually is, per Lesson 4.
right: A guardrail that sets the maximum permissions any identity in an account or OU can ever have
One invoice across every member account, with volume discounts calculated on combined usage
The all-powerful identity created with every AWS account, reserved for setup rather than daily use
A folder-like grouping of accounts inside an Organization, used to apply policy in bulk
questions.explain: The root user is the all-powerful identity tied to every account's signup email, reserved for setup rather than daily use. An OU is a folder-like grouping of accounts inside an Organization for applying policy in bulk. An SCP is a guardrail that caps the maximum permissions available inside an account or OU, no matter what its own IAM policies say. Consolidated billing gives one invoice across every member account, with volume discounts on combined usage.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: AWS's security responsibility covers the physical data centers, hardware, host OS, and global network infrastructure — this half of the split is called security ________ the cloud.
questions.explain: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud — the physical facilities, hardware, host OS, and global network backbone. The customer is responsible for everything configured on top of that, called security IN the cloud.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes an AWS IAM role, as distinct from an IAM user?
options: A role has no long-term credentials of its own — it's assumed temporarily and receives short-lived credentials from AWS STS
A role is a password-protected identity meant for one specific person's daily console login
A role is simply another name for an IAM group once a policy is attached to it
A role can only be assumed by a human user, never by an AWS service
A role's credentials, once issued, never expire until someone manually revokes them
A role must always carry the exact same permissions as the account's root user
questions.explain: An IAM role carries no long-term credentials at all — no password, no access keys. It's assumed by a person, application, or AWS service, which receives temporary, auto-expiring credentials via AWS STS. This is exactly why roles, not long-lived user access keys, are the default recommended way for one AWS service to call another.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes an IAM user, not a role — a password for console sign-in is exactly the kind of long-term credential a user carries and a role deliberately never has. Mixing up which one holds a password versus which one is temporarily assumed is the core distinction this lesson is testing.

questions.prompt: A data pipeline needs a small piece of code that runs for a few seconds whenever a new file lands in S3, and does nothing the rest of the time. Per Lesson 7, which compute choice fits this, and why?
options: Lambda — it's event-triggered and billed only for actual invocation time, with nothing running and nothing billed between triggers
EC2 — because only EC2 instances are able to read from S3 at all
Lambda — because Lambda functions run continuously in the background by default, waiting for events
EC2 — because Lambda has no maximum execution time, which makes it riskier for a short task
questions.explain: Lambda runs code in response to an event, like an S3 upload, and bills only for the actual compute time used, down to the millisecond, with nothing running or billed while idle. This is exactly the short, event-driven shape Lesson 7 says Lambda fits well — the opposite of EC2's continuously-running, billed-while-idle model.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about S3 versus EBS, per Lesson 8.
options: S3 objects are accessed via an HTTP(S) API using a key, not mounted as a filesystem
An EBS volume can typically be attached to only one EC2 instance at a time
An EBS volume lives in exactly one Availability Zone
S3 is the default choice for a data pipeline's raw and staged files because it isn't tied to any one compute instance
EBS has no practical size limit and can be queried directly by Athena the same way an S3 bucket can
questions.explain: S3 objects are addressed by key over HTTPS, not mounted like a disk. An EBS volume lives in one specific AZ and, with rare exceptions, attaches to only one instance at a time. S3's decoupling from any one instance is exactly why it's the default landing zone for pipeline data. EBS is block storage sized per volume, not the practically-unlimited, directly-queryable-by-Athena object storage that S3 is — that description belongs to S3, not EBS.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: what actually makes a subnet "public" in a VPC isn't a label on the subnet itself — it's whether its ________ sends internet-bound traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to an Internet Gateway.
questions.explain: A subnet is public specifically because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an Internet Gateway attached to the VPC. A private subnet's route table simply has no such route — there's no separate 'public/private' flag on the subnet itself.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: AWS's deepest compute discount comes from ________ Instances — bidding on AWS's spare capacity, with the tradeoff that AWS can reclaim the instance on short notice.
questions.explain: Spot Instances offer the steepest discount of the EC2 pricing models by using AWS's spare capacity, appropriate for fault-tolerant or flexible workloads that can handle being interrupted and resumed — unlike Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, which trade a 1-3 year commitment for a smaller, steadier discount.

questions.prompt: An IAM identity has one policy statement with Effect: Allow for a given action on a resource, and a separate policy statement with Effect: Deny for that exact same action on that exact same resource. What's the result?
options: The action is denied — an explicit Deny anywhere always overrides an Allow from elsewhere
The action is allowed, because Allow statements take priority over Deny statements
AWS raises an error at evaluation time because the two policies conflict
Whichever policy was attached most recently wins, regardless of its Effect
The action is allowed only if the Deny statement happens to be an inline policy rather than a managed policy
IAM averages the two statements together and grants partial, read-only permission
questions.explain: IAM's evaluation order is unambiguous: an explicit Deny anywhere always wins, regardless of how many Allow statements exist elsewhere, and if nothing explicitly allows an action the implicit default deny applies. There's no averaging, no error, and no priority based on which policy was attached last or what type it is.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B gets the priority exactly backwards. It's tempting to assume more permissive statements win, but IAM is deliberately built the opposite way — an explicit Deny is the one thing that can never be overridden by an Allow, precisely so a guardrail policy can't be quietly defeated by a broader grant attached somewhere else.

questions.prompt: This policy is attached to a role that, in practice, only ever calls s3:GetObject on one specific bucket. Per Lesson 13, is this policy an example of least privilege?
options: No — least privilege means granting exactly the actions and resources actually needed, regardless of which ones happen to get used in practice
Yes — since the role never actually calls any other action, the broader grant causes no real harm
Yes — because s3:* is required just to be able to call s3:GetObject at all
No, but only because Resource: "*" is technically invalid JSON syntax
questions.explain: Least privilege is judged by what a policy grants, not by what the role happens to use. A policy granting every S3 action on every bucket is a least-privilege violation even if the role's real-world calls only ever touch s3:GetObject on one bucket — Lesson 13 names this exact pattern as the single most common least-privilege violation in real AWS accounts.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about IAM users, groups, and roles, per Lesson 11.
options: An IAM group can have policies attached directly, but it has no credentials of its own and can't be assumed
An IAM user's access keys and console password are long-term credentials that don't expire on their own
An IAM group can be nested inside another IAM group
A role's temporary credentials are issued by AWS STS and expire automatically
A role is the best fit for a human who needs day-to-day console and CLI access
questions.explain: A group is purely an administrative convenience — no credentials, can't be logged into or assumed, and groups cannot be nested inside other groups. A user's password and access keys are long-term credentials that don't expire on their own, which is exactly why a leaked one is risky. A role's credentials come from AWS STS and expire automatically. Day-to-day human access is Lesson 11's example for an IAM user in a group, not a role.

questions.prompt: Match each policy-related term to what it actually is, per Lesson 12.
right: Embedded directly in one identity, not reusable, and deleted along with that identity
Attached to the resource itself and includes a Principal element naming who it grants access to
Attached directly to a user, group, or role
Written and maintained by AWS, convenient to start with but often broader than a pipeline needs
questions.explain: An identity-based policy is attached directly to a user, group, or role. A resource-based policy is attached to the resource itself and is the one policy type that names a Principal, since it isn't already attached to the identity it concerns. An AWS managed policy is written and maintained by AWS — convenient, but often wider than a real pipeline needs. An inline policy is embedded in one identity, not reusable, and disappears with that identity.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a human in Account A getting temporary access to a role in Account B in the correct order, per Lesson 14.
items: Account B creates a role with a trust policy naming Account A as a trusted Principal
The human in Account A calls sts:AssumeRole against that role's ARN
STS returns temporary credentials scoped to Account B's role, valid for up to an hour by default
The human in Account A acts using those temporary credentials, having never held standing access to Account B
questions.explain: Account B first has to create the role and name Account A as a trusted Principal in its trust policy. Only then can the human in Account A call sts:AssumeRole against that role's ARN. STS responds with temporary, time-limited credentials, and the human uses those — at no point did Account A's user hold any permanent, standing access to Account B.

questions.prompt: A data engineer runs aws s3 cp file.csv s3://my-bucket/raw/ and it fails with AccessDenied. Per Lesson 15, what actually determines whether this command succeeds?
options: The IAM identity behind the active AWS CLI profile's credentials, and whether its policy actually allows the underlying s3:PutObject action
Whether the AWS CLI itself has administrator rights by default
Whether the file being uploaded is smaller than 5 GB
Whether aws configure was run more recently than the aws s3 cp command
questions.explain: Every aws CLI command reads credentials from the active profile, and whatever IAM identity those credentials belong to — and its attached policy — is exactly what determines which commands succeed and which return AccessDenied. The CLI itself has no inherent permissions beyond whatever that IAM identity is actually granted.

questions.prompt: This code runs inside a Lambda function with no credentials passed to boto3.client(), and it works. Per Lesson 16, why does this work without any hardcoded access key?
options: boto3 searches the credential chain and finds the IAM role attached to the Lambda function's execution role, picking up its temporary credentials automatically
Lambda functions are exempt from IAM entirely
boto3.client() defaults to full administrator access whenever no credentials are explicitly supplied
S3 doesn't require any authentication for a boto3 call
questions.explain: boto3 searches a fixed credential chain, and the IAM role attached to the compute running the code — here, the Lambda function's execution role — is the last and most commonly relied-on link in that chain for pipeline code. The code never needs an explicit key because the execution role's temporary credentials are already available to it automatically.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Associate-tier certification most directly aligned with this course's data engineering track is AWS Certified ________ – Associate.
questions.explain: AWS Certified Data Engineer – Associate tests exactly the territory this course and the AWS Data Engineering course that follows it are built around: data ingestion, transformation, storage, and orchestration on AWS. Lesson 18 also notes it replaced an older Specialty-tier data credential.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the AWS CLI and the SDK (boto3), per Lessons 15 and 16.
options: The CLI and boto3 ultimately call the exact same underlying AWS APIs
boto3's client interface maps nearly 1:1 onto each API action and exists for every service
boto3's resource interface is available for every single AWS service, with no exceptions
Forgetting --profile on an AWS CLI command silently falls back to the [default] profile
The credential chain's very first priority is always the IAM role attached to the compute running the code
questions.explain: The CLI and boto3 are two interfaces over the same APIs. The client interface is the near-literal, always-available mapping onto every action. The resource interface, by contrast, is only available for a subset of services, not every one. Forgetting --profile really does silently fall back to [default], a classic source of 'wrong account' confusion. The credential chain actually checks explicit in-code credentials first (discouraged, but still first), then environment variables, then the shared credentials file, and only then the attached IAM role — so the role is not the chain's first priority, just the one real pipelines end up relying on.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Lesson 17 S3 deploy walkthrough in the correct order.
items: Create the bucket with aws s3 mb s3://bucket-name --region us-east-1
Upload a file into it with aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://bucket-name/
List the bucket's contents to confirm the object is there with aws s3 ls s3://bucket-name/
Download the object to stdout to confirm its contents with aws s3 cp s3://bucket-name/hello.txt -
Delete the object with aws s3 rm, then remove the now-empty bucket with aws s3 rb
questions.explain: The walkthrough runs mb (make bucket) first, then cp to upload a file, then verifies with ls and a stdout cp rather than just assuming the upload worked, and only then cleans up — rm to delete the object, since rb only works on an already-empty bucket, then rb to remove the bucket itself.
